item.title: Vascular Waveform Analysis Using Bayesian Pulse Deconvolution — Wed Oct 14, 1:00 PM — None
item.description:
Abstract: Vascular waveforms such as arterial pressure, photoplethysmography, and tonometry are widely used to measure vital signs, diagnose conditions, and predict long-term health outcomes. However, the analysis of these signals typically relies on heuristic filtering and signal processing operations that encode unexamined assumptions and introduce cascading errors and artifacts. Instead, we propose Bayesian pulse deconvolution as a flexible method for analyzing vascular waveforms informed by biological and physical domain knowledge. Across simulated waveforms and real human recordings we find this method significantly outperforms standard signal processing pipelines for filtering noise, detecting pulse times, and extracting pulse shapes.In this talk, I will explain the method and reflect on the advantages of analyzing human biosignals using Bayesian methods that encode domain knowledge and quantify uncertainty.

item.title: Inbal Abergil | Artist Talk — Wed Oct 14, 1:30 PM — Center for Documentary Studies
item.description:
Making Peace with Death: What War Leaves Behind Inbal Abergil with guest Tracy Dice-Johnson Center for Documentary Studies Auditorium 1317 W. Pettigrew Street, Durham. October 14th, 1:30-2:30pm
Documentary photographer Inbal Abergil will present her work examining the aftermath of war through grief, memory, and remembrance. Through her projects "Making Peace with Death", "N.O.K.-Next of Kin", and "The Presence of Absence", Abergil documents the people, objects, and memories shaped by loss. Her photographs include portraits of Casualty Notification Officers and military chaplains, personal belongings left behind, and testimonies from Gold Star families. Her work explores how personal objects hold memory, how loss continues across generations, and the human cost of conflict for those who endure it.

item.title: CDVS Workshop: Preparing for Data Publishing: Standards and Disciplinary Repositories (General Case Studies) — Thu Oct 15, 10:00 AM — Online
item.description:
Research data have value beyond their original purpose and by sharing or "publishing" your data you can support open science, reproducibility, and future innovation. This workshop will explore strategies and best practices for formally publishing your data in a data repository. Topics covered will include new modes of publishing in academia, the use of data and metadata standards to support interoperability and harmonization, an overview of repository options and key features, examples of disciplinary repositories, and data publishing methods to increase the impact of research projects and support the FAIR Guiding Principles (i.e., Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable). Participants will engage in a break-out activity where they will practice finding and assessing data repositories using a general case study. This event is open to non-Duke participants. This workshop is eligible for 2 hours of Graduate School RCR Credit (GS714) and 200-level faculty and staff RCR.

item.title: Exhibit Opening of "Playhouses and Picture Palaces: The Historical Theaters of Downtown Durham," — Fri Oct 16, 6:00 PM — Museum of Durham History
item.description:
Join us at the Museum of Durham History at 6:00 pm for the opening of “Playhouses and Picture Palaces: The Historical Theaters of Downtown Durham,” our new exhibit on the theaters of Durham. The exhibit traces the evolution of Durham’s entertainment landscape from its earliest opera houses and playhouses to the elaborate “picture palaces” that emerged during the golden age of cinema.This includes the experiences of Black Durham residents, including the important role theaters in the thriving Hayti community played in providing spaces for Black audiences and performers during the Jim Crow era of segregation. This event is free and open to people of all ages. We will have music by jazz students from North Carolina Central University and free snacks.

item.title: Fraser Fir Transplanting Workday (Burnsville) — Tue Oct 20, 10:00 AM
item.description:
Join NCWF alongside Southern Appalachian Spruce Restoration Initiative partners to help transplant fraser fir trees at Mt Mitchell State Park. We’re relocating the trees to an area in the park that we’re aiming to reforest and restore to spruce-fir habitat. Spruce-fir habitat in North Carolina is a rare, ice-age relict ecosystem found exclusively on mountain peaks above 5,000 feet. Characterized by red spruce and Fraser fir trees, it mimics the Canadian boreal forest and supports specialized wildlife like the Carolina northern flying squirrel and spruce-fir moss spider.
REGISTER HERE

item.title: MEMS Seminar: Gregory S. Rohrer, "How Flat Grain Boundaries Influence Microstructure Evolution in Polycrystals." — Wed Oct 14, 12:00 PM — Fitzpatrick Center Schiciano Auditorium Side A
item.description:
The Thomas Lord Department of Mechanical Engineering and Materials Science welcomes Professor Gregory S. Rohrer (Carnegie Mellon) to deliver the MEMS Seminar, "How Flat Grain Boundaries Influence Microstructure Evolution in Polycrystals."
ABSTRACT: Recent studies of grain growth in polycrystals by three-dimensional high energy X-ray diffraction microscopy have been able to quantify grain boundary migration rates in a variety of materials. One of the principal findings has been that grain boundary curvature is not a good predictor of the direction or speed of grain boundary migration, overturning what was considered a governing principle of microstructure evolution. Another surprising result is the fastest observed grain boundaries are also the flattest, having zero curvature within the resolution of the measurement. item.title: Accountable Care in 2027: Building the Evidence Base and Driving Practical Policy Solutions — Wed Oct 14, 1:00 PM — None
item.description:
As 2027 approaches, accountable care is entering a new phase of evolution. While the model has largely proven more effective than traditional fee-for-service payment, there is less agreement on what comes next. Join Duke-Margolis and West Health on October 14 for an event that will explore progress in accountable care to-date and opportunities to leverage evidence to accelerate accountable care.
Accountable care is now a permanent part of the Medicare landscape, yet its future impact will depend on policymakers' ability to modernize the data, technology, and payment infrastructure that supports it. The next phase may be defined not by voluntary expansion, but by the permanent adoption of evidence-based approaches that can be rapidly tested, refined, and scaled across the health care system.
Source: Duke University
